core: Mise-en-scène as the visible arrangement presented for the camera
Setting, props, costume and character appearance, lighting, and composition as analytic lenses
A descriptive-before-interpretive method for making qualified visual claims
supporting: The theatrical origin of the term
Overlap and distinction among mise-en-scène, cinematography, editing, and sound
How recurrence and arrangement can support a visual interpretation
outOfScope: Detailed technical instruction in lighting, lenses, camera movement, editing, or sound design
Film history surveys, auteur theory, or claims about a filmmaker's private intention
Analysis of copyrighted films or reproduction of film images

claims.claim: Mise-en-scène is a term with theatrical origins that film analysis uses for what is placed or arranged before the camera, including objects, sets, costumes, and performers.
An introductory account of mise-en-scène can examine setting, character appearance, lighting, and composition as connected elements of visual design.
Setting analysis can attend to designed space and objects, while costume, hair, and makeup contribute to visible character appearance.
Composition concerns the arrangement of people, objects, and setting within the frame; for moving images, framing and movement are relevant to that arrangement.
A formal viewing method can begin with observations about what appears in the frame before developing an interpretation of patterns across a sequence.
Mise-en-scène intersects with cinematography but does not exhaust film form: camera distance, movement, lenses, editing, and sound pose additional analytic questions.
A visual technique does not carry one universal meaning; an interpretation is stronger when it identifies concrete evidence and states its limits.

sourceRecords.title: How to Watch a Film
sourceRecords.notes: Official MIT OpenCourseWare course handout read as a PDF. It also supplies the broader formal-analysis context. The lesson uses original synthesis only.
